title: Generic-fibre specialization rectangles and chain lifting
statement:
Let $h:Y\to X$ be a regular morphism between Noetherian excellent schemes [def-exc-excellent-ring], meaning flat with geometrically regular fibres (the fibres remain regular after every finite extension of the residue field) [def-weil-flat-morphism, def-weil-regular-scheme, def-pc-scheme-fibre]. Use geometric specializations and codimension after strict localization as in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex, def-weil-geometric-point, def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. Given a geometric specialization $\bar y'\rightsquigarrow\bar y$ above $\bar x'\rightsquigarrow\bar x$, there is a commutative square of geometric specializations
$$\begin{array}{ccc}\bar\eta'&\rightsquigarrow&\bar\eta\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ \bar y'&\rightsquigarrow&\bar y\end{array}$$
with the vertical arrows in the fibres over $\bar x'$ and $\bar x$ and with $\bar\eta',\bar\eta$ of codimension zero in those fibres. The top specialization has the codimension of $\bar x'\rightsquigarrow\bar x$. Any chosen finite saturated factorization of the base specialization lifts to a factorization of the top specialization with every intermediate point of codimension zero in its fibre and every lifted arrow of the same codimension as its base arrow. A saturated factorization has immediate arrows, with a codimension-zero transport allowed at the ends.

Put $c_h(y)=\dim\mathcal O_{Y_{h(y)},y}$, using local-ring Krull dimension [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. The two vertical arrows have codimensions $c_h(y')$ and $c_h(y)$, respectively, and codimensions add along either path in the square. Thus, if the given bottom and base arrows have codimensions $b$ and $a$,
$$c_h(y')+b=a+c_h(y).$$
These assertions hold after the compatible strict localizations determined by the specified arrows; no assertion that an arbitrary global geometric fibre is connected is made.

source.place: Expose XVII, Lemmas 4.3.2.3–4.3.2.6 (strict-local fibre integrality, lifting with preserved codimension, chains, and square); Expose XIV, Proposition 2.5.4 (codimension relation); additivity in excellent strict localizations.

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-regular-specialization-geometry] with $r=h$, $P=Y$, $t'=\bar y'$ and $t=\bar y$. Its hypotheses are exactly the present Noetherian excellence and regularity hypotheses, and its geometric specializations and codimensions use the same strict-localization convention. Its rectangle assertion supplies fibre-generic $\bar\eta',\bar\eta$ and the two fibrewise vertical arrows. It asserts equality of the two composites to $\bar y$, so this is a square of the specified geometric arrows, not only of their underlying points. Fibre-generic means codimension zero in the corresponding fibre, as required.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.6, printed p.285; use the existing stronger geometry node.

proof.text: Both endpoints of the top arrow obtained in Step 1 are fibre-generic. The generic-lift clause of [lem-per-regular-specialization-geometry] says that a fibre-generic lift ending at $\bar\eta$ of the base arrow is unique up to isomorphism and has the base codimension $a$. Hence the top arrow has codimension $a$. Given a chosen finite saturated base factorization, its immediate-arrow factorization clause lifts that factorization of this top arrow through fibre-generic points, with each lifted arrow immediate. Therefore each such arrow has codimension one, equal to its base arrow. If the chosen factorization includes codimension-zero transports at its ends, separate off those geometric isomorphisms first, apply this clause to the immediate part, and compose back the endpoint isomorphisms. The identity and geometric-isomorphism cases are explicitly allowed by the same cited statement; they have codimension zero and do not change either the intermediate fibre-generic condition or any codimension.

In the notation $b(t)$ of [lem-per-regular-specialization-geometry], $b(t)=c_h(t)$ by their identical local-ring definitions. Its final clause therefore gives vertical codimensions $c_h(y')$ and $c_h(y)$. For the bottom arrow its displayed codimension identity reads $b=a+c_h(y)-c_h(y')$. All dimensions here are finite local-ring dimensions, so rearranging gives $c_h(y')+b=a+c_h(y)$. In particular this is equality of the sums along the two paths in the square.

source.place: XIV, Proposition 2.5.4 and XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.6; rearrangement of the existing geometry-node identity.

proof.text: To check that both path sums are also the codimension of their common composite, apply the same displayed identity of [lem-per-regular-specialization-geometry] to the geometric arrow $\bar\eta'\rightsquigarrow\bar y$ (either composite, equal by Step 1). Its base arrow is $\bar x'\rightsquigarrow\bar x$ of codimension $a$, and $c_h(\eta')=0$ since $\eta'$ is fibre-generic. The identity gives $c_Y(\bar\eta',\bar y)=a+c_h(y)$. This is the sum along the upper and right edges by Steps 2 and 3, and equals $c_h(y')+b$, the sum along the left and bottom edges, by Step 3. Thus codimensions add along both paths. Every cited assertion uses the compatible strict localizations of the specified geometric arrows; the proof makes no connectedness assertion about a global fibre.

source.place: XIV, Proposition 2.5.4; codimension identity applied to the common composite from XVII, Lemma 4.3.2.6.
